name: Monster Walks with Band Around Ankles
description: Monster walks are a dynamic hip abductor exercise performed by walking laterally with a resistance band looped around the ankles. Maintaining a quarter-squat position throughout keeps constant tension on the hip abductors. This exercise is commonly used in warm-up protocols and rehabilitation to strengthen the gluteus medius, improve lateral hip stability, and address knee valgus patterns during athletic movement.

execution.starting_position: Place a resistance band around both ankles. Stand with feet hip-width apart in a quarter-squat position — knees slightly bent, hips pushed back slightly, chest tall.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band that creates meaningful resistance without causing the torso to tip side to side during each step. Clear a path of at least 3-4 meters for lateral movement.
steps: Step 1: Adopt a quarter-squat stance with the band taut between the ankles.
Step 2: Step laterally with the lead foot, widening the stance beyond shoulder width.
Step 3: Follow with the trail foot, returning to shoulder-width — do not let feet come fully together.
Step 4: Continue for the prescribed distance or steps, then repeat in the opposite direction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. Exhale on each step if needed; do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to sway laterally with each step
Letting feet come fully together (releases band tension)
Standing fully upright rather than maintaining the squat position
safety_considerations: If you have knee pain, reduce band resistance and ensure knees track over toes
Stop if you feel hip flexor cramping — reduce range or band resistance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Each lateral step should be wide enough to maintain continuous band tension. Avoid shuffling with feet too close together.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled — 1 second per step, maintaining consistent tension throughout
coaching_cues: Stay low throughout — do not bob up and down
Drive through the outer hip to step, not the knee
Keep toes pointing forward — avoid external rotation compensation
